desc:
For a node x, look at the values of x and all its descendants. The subtree average of x is the sum of those values divided by how many there are, rounded down to an integer.

Return how many nodes have a value equal to their own subtree average. The empty tree gives 0.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [3, 1, 2] the average at the root is 6 / 3 = 2, which differs from 3, while both leaves equal their own value, so the answer is 2. For [2, 1, 3] the root's average is 2, so all three nodes count and the answer is 3.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: For one node you need two numbers from its subtree: the sum of values and the number of nodes.
Both numbers of a node are the node's own contribution plus the numbers of its two children, so they can be accumulated bottom-up.
Go through the real nodes from last to first, keeping sum[k] and cnt[k]. Count the nodes with sum[k] // cnt[k] == value[k] (all values are non-negative, so // rounds down).
editorial: Re-summing the subtree of every node is O(n<sup>2</sup>) on a path. Instead keep two totals per node: the sum of values in its subtree and the number of nodes. A node's totals are its own value and 1 plus the totals of its children.

In the level-order array children follow their parent, so a backward pass over the real nodes always finds the children's totals ready. After computing a node's totals, compare sum // cnt with the node's value. Total sums are at most 1,500 × 10,000 = 15 million, well within 32 bits.
